text: The war here runs on a schedule, and the people cast as the enemy clock in for it. Inside a military role-playing facility, an actress who hopes the job leads somewhere real falls for a soldier assigned to play an insurgent, and what passes between them will not stay inside the script. Hailey Benton Gates keeps two sets of books for 103 minutes: every gesture has to serve the exercise and serve something else, and only one of the two is being graded. The stakes are odd and precise. An arrangement designed so that nothing can be lost turns out to have something to lose, because the whole apparatus depends on nobody meaning it. Comedy and drama are both listed, which for a place that hires civilians to lose a war on command is less a hedge than an accurate description.

A newcomer starts his own show on the local cable channel and opens by asking what is wrong with the town. Brewster has no obvious answer; it is peaceful, harmonious and pleased with itself, which is exactly the condition Whiley Pritcher's question is built to test. Bryan Singer took the U.S. Dramatic Grand Jury Prize at Sundance with a thriller built from the cheapest instrument available — a camera, a slot on the schedule, and whoever picks up the phone. The escalation is in the wording. What is wrong becomes who is wrong. Nothing in the format requires evidence, only airtime, and 86 minutes leaves no room to survey the town at leisure: the portrait gets drawn entirely out of what people are willing to say on air. That is a more damning method than any survey would be.

Two children meet on the street, and one of them starts teaching the other how to take things without paying. Lonnie is twelve and carefully raised. Karen defers to nobody, and the curriculum runs to makeup, skipped school, small thefts, and lies told at home that get confessed to a priest later on. Marisa Silver lets the traffic run both ways — some honesty goes back in the other direction — which keeps 92 minutes of minor transgression from hardening into a lesson. The scale stays honest; nothing at stake is larger than an afternoon unaccounted for or a small thing taken off a shelf. Class is the subject, and it stays where a child actually meets it: in who is expected home for supper, in whose parents can be lied to safely, in what one house permits that another does not.

Everything on the list gets done: the hall, the tuxedo, the rings. Nancy Savoca puts the machinery of a wedding in the foreground and keeps the two people slightly behind it, which turns out to be the honest arrangement, since Donna and Michael have less say in the event than the event has in them. He is not ready to be married. She has noticed, and has doubts of her own that she is not raising. Cold feet on both sides, and a hall already booked. Sundance gave the film its U.S. Dramatic Grand Jury Prize, and whatever the jury saw is legible in the errands: 104 minutes of tasks, each too small to argue about, accumulating into a decision neither party has quite made. The comedy is in the arrangements. The drama is in what the arrangements are for.

A woman takes a man on the street for a director whose name she knows, and the mistake is allowed to stand. From there, Sunday is two strangers maintaining a useful fiction: a British actress whose career has stalled, asking for help; a homeless man handed a better identity than his own and given no reason to return it. Jonathan Nossiter spends 91 minutes on a premise that could collapse in ten, and the tension is entirely a matter of duration — how long a lie stays worth the trouble when the alternative is the day each of them actually has. It took the Waldo Salt Screenwriting Award and the U.S. Dramatic Grand Jury Prize at Sundance, along with the Grand prix du Festival de Deauville: three prizes for a film made of talk between people who have agreed not to check anything.

A weekend reunion for married couples, run on methods frankly described as terrible and reported to work — usually. That qualifier is the hook, and Bobby Roth's thriller lives on it. It is filed as a thriller, though the danger is procedural rather than physical. Nothing intrudes from outside; the pressure is a procedure applied to people who know one another socially and will have to keep sitting in the same room afterwards, each holding the thing the procedure exists to extract. Ninety-seven minutes is enough to run it on more than one marriage, which is where a premise this schematic either finds a second gear or does not. Everyone here signed up, more or less, and the interest is in the moment a person understands what they agreed to and stays in the chair anyway.

Alice tends to Gertrude, who is ill, and the visitors keep arriving. Jill Godmilow calls her portrait of Stein and Toklas fictionalized, which frees it from any duty to prove things: a summer in France in the 1930s, Fernande Olivier and Guillaume Apollinaire to be called on, Hemingway putting his head round the door. What the invention buys is the ordinary hours. A legend has a shape and demands to be serviced; a day does not, and the day is what this film wants. Two people who have been talking to each other for decades do not explain themselves for anyone's benefit, so the work happens in shorthand, in silences, in the management of a sick friend's schedule. Sundance gave it the U.S. Dramatic Grand Jury Prize. Eighty-eight minutes, almost all of it company.

A president goes on television to say he will not run again, and a dorm room celebrates by getting stoned. The broadcast is LBJ's. The celebration lasts about as long as it takes the neighbour they have pelted with junk food to call the police, and within minutes Matt and his roommates are off campus for good. David Burton Morris runs that chain at speed, because the point is the disproportion: a piece of small, stupid, entirely ordinary trouble, and behind it a country that has arranged for the consequence to be a war. What follows is a return home and the business of a house that now contains a son who is no longer a student. The comedy is real, and it is not a cushion. Ninety-seven minutes, a prank and a war on one line of causation, and only one of them open to negotiation.

One line of story and 98 minutes to spend inside it: a love affair coming apart, and a man who cannot keep his jealousy out of the frame. Rob Nilsson has chosen the least sympathetic position available in a romance — not the person being left, exactly, but the person whose conduct is becoming the subject — and stays there well past the point where most films cut away to somebody else's afternoon. That is a commitment rather than a plot. Romance is listed as a genre, which here means the aftermath of one rather than the making of it. What the film offers is proximity, harder to sustain than incident and much harder to make bearable. It carried the U.S. Dramatic Grand Jury Prize out of Sundance. Rage is easy to photograph and difficult to observe honestly.

A jury at Sundance gave its top dramatic prize to a comedy about a writer whose manuscript keeps coming back. Dick Kendred cannot place the book, and the diagnosis he is offered, in the crude shorthand of the trade, is that it needs more sex; he then takes a room in a house with two women who are not difficult to interest. Gary Walkow files the picture under science fiction as well as comedy, and that is the detail to hold onto — whatever Dick is writing does not stay on the page, and 86 minutes have to carry a farce and an invented world at once. Tom Villard plays him. The joke underneath is a sturdy one: the block is never about the book, and everything done to break it ends up in the manuscript.

A child sees something in Golden Gate Park that she was not meant to see, and afterwards she is the one who becomes hard to be near. Beth de Araújo builds 119 minutes on that inversion. The crime is finished early; the damage is a household matter, negotiated between two parents who want justice and, more urgently, want a room that feels safe. Josephine is eight, and her method of protection is to strike first at whatever is closest, which leaves the adults prosecuting one thing while managing another. Justice, in this arrangement, is the part of the problem that comes with a procedure. Drama, crime and thriller are all listed, in that order, and the order is right. What is under test is whether a family can absorb a shock without passing it around.

Rome in summer, emptied out and glaring, and a man on a Vespa with nowhere he has to be. That is the first of three diary entries, and it establishes the method: Nanni Moretti rides, looks at buildings and neighbourhoods, says plainly what he thinks of them, and lets the city stay a city. The second entry leaves for an island and then keeps leaving, island to islet, chasing a quiet that recedes at the speed it is pursued. The third turns to a body producing symptoms nobody can name. Nothing is dramatised in the usual sense; the unit of construction is the observation, delivered dry, and the structure is the order in which the observations arrived. It holds the David di Donatello for Best Film and a place on the TSPDT 1,000, and never raises its voice to get them.

The village has no water, and the only plan anyone has is to go down into the ground and look for it. Wu Tianming gives Old Well a hundred and twenty-nine minutes, most of them spent on labour — rock, rope, the specific weight of work an entire settlement depends on and that pays nothing while it is underway. The romance is not a separate track. A married man and the woman he did not marry end up in the same shaft when it collapses, and the enclosure does what conversation had not managed. Feeling, here, surfaces only when the work stops. Three domestic prizes followed: Golden Rooster, Hundred Flowers, Huabiao. It sits on the Golden Horse list of the hundred greatest Chinese-language films. Digging is filmed as digging, and it takes the time it takes.

One of them talks constantly and believes she is admired; the other watches, copies, and says almost nothing. They work the same job, then take the same rooms, and what follows stops resembling a roommate arrangement fairly quickly. Robert Altman spends 124 minutes letting imitation turn into something for which nobody on screen has a word. The asymmetry is the engine: admiration is the most invasive thing one person can direct at another, and the younger of the two has no practice at moderating it. Very little gets explained, and the refusal is deliberate rather than coy. The record has held — an acting prize, a place on the TSPDT 1,000 — though the reason to watch is smaller and stranger: the exactness with which two people who cannot say what they want are observed.
